1.title: Other Existing Laws Applied to AI
1.text: Welcome to Module five: Other Existing Laws Applied to A I. Competency B of domain two asks how laws that were not written for A I still apply to it. Four areas matter: intellectual property, nondiscrimination, consumer protection, and product liability. Several of the points here are still developing, so watch for the verify-live tags.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Explain how intellectual property law limits what data A I may train on, and who owns outputs. Explain how nondiscrimination law reaches hiring, credit, housing and insurance. Explain how consumer protection law treats unfair and deceptive A I claims. And explain how product liability law treats A I defects, including the new E U rules.

1.title: Case Check-In: Training Data, Hiring Results and a Marketing Claim
1.text: At Helios, three things happen at once. The support assistant learned from help-center articles, some written by third parties. The hiring tool selects one group of applicants at a clearly lower rate than another. And marketing wants to call the assistant always accurate, although it once gave a customer a refund window that does not exist. Jonas Weber, Head of Legal and Privacy, asks which laws beyond privacy are now in play.

1.title: How Intellectual Property Law Meets AI
1.text: Intellectual property law meets A I at several points. Copyright protects creative works, so it bears on training data and on outputs that copy. Patents protect inventions, and courts and offices have required a human inventor. Trade secrets and confidentiality protect model weights, prompts and data, and leaks to public tools destroy secrecy. Trademarks and likeness protect names, logos and personal identity. And contracts and licenses can limit data use even where law would allow it. Exam tip: first name the right being used, then ask whether use is allowed.

1.title: Training Data: Copyright, Mining Exceptions and Opt-Outs
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. In the U S, copyright allows fair use, decided case by case on four factors: purpose and character of the use, nature of the work, amount used, and effect on the market. In the E U, there are exceptions for text and data mining, but a rightsholder can reserve its rights. Providers of general-purpose models must have a copyright policy that honors such reservations, and must publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content, under Article fifty-three. Website terms and dataset licenses can restrict use even where an exception exists. Exam tip: public availability is not permission.

1.title: Outputs: Who Owns What AI Makes?
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide, tagged verify live. Copyright needs human authorship. Purely A I-generated material is not protected, while human-written parts and creative selection, arrangement or editing can be. The U S Copyright Office released its report on copyrightability on the twenty-ninth of January, twenty twenty-five, and said prompts alone were not enough. An A I cannot be a patent inventor. Outputs can also infringe, so the user or company may face a claim. Contracts decide the rest: who owns outputs, and who indemnifies. As of the twenty-seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, these rules are still being refined.

1.title: Licenses, Trade Secrets and Confidentiality
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Open-source licenses: permissive ones allow wide reuse, while copyleft ones can require sharing derived code on the same terms. Model licenses: open weights are not always open source, and use restrictions are common. Dataset licenses limit purposes, such as research only. Trade secrets cover weights, prompts and training recipes, and need reasonable secrecy measures. Staff pasting client or personal data into public tools can breach contracts and destroy secrecy. At Helios, that means an approved-tools list and license review for every model and dataset. Exam tip: read the license.

1.title: Where the Courts Stand
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide, tagged dates and verify live. On the twenty-ninth of September, twenty twenty-six, the Third Circuit affirmed the ruling against Ross in Thomson Reuters. It is the first federal appellate decision on fair use in A I training, but the tool was not generative, and the court did not hold that training is always infringing. In Bartz against Anthropic, training on lawfully acquired books was held fair use, keeping pirated copies was not, and the case settled for one point five billion dollars. Overall, there is no controlling appellate ruling on generative training. Exam tip: fair use is fact-specific.

1.title: Two Theories of Discrimination
1.text: Discrimination law has two main theories. Disparate treatment means treating people differently because of a protected characteristic, such as race, color, religion, sex or national origin, under Title VII. Disparate impact means a neutral practice that falls harder on a protected group. It is unlawful if it is not job related and consistent with business necessity, or if a less discriminatory alternative exists. In A I, proxies such as a postal code can cause impact without using the characteristic. Age and disability are covered too. Exam tip: if the tool never sees the characteristic but results differ, think disparate impact.

1.title: Measuring Adverse Impact: The Four-Fifths Rule
1.text: How do you measure adverse impact? Selection rate is the share of a group's applicants who are selected. The impact ratio is the lower group's rate divided by the highest group's rate. A ratio below four-fifths, or eighty percent, is generally treated by federal agencies as evidence of adverse impact, under the Uniform Guidelines. It is a rule of thumb, not a safe harbor. For example, fifty percent against thirty percent gives zero point six. Forty of one hundred against thirty-six of one hundred gives zero point nine. Exam tip: compute lower over higher.

1.title: Employment: Screening Tools and the Vendor's Role
1.text: Employers answer for the tools they use to screen, rank or reject applicants. Vendors can be drawn in. In Mobley against Workday, a U S court let claims proceed on the theory that an A I hiring vendor can act as an agent of its employer customers. On the sixteenth of May, twenty twenty-five, the court allowed an age-discrimination collective to start. Tools that screen out disabled applicants raise A D A risk. Governance means testing for adverse impact before and after launch, keeping human review, and asking vendors for validation evidence. As of the twenty-seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, the case was still pending.

1.title: Credit, Lending, Housing and Insurance
1.text: Credit and lending: the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and Regulation B require notice of action within thirty days of a completed application, with specific principal reasons. Saying only that the applicant failed a credit score is insufficient. Housing: the Fair Housing Act covers tenant screening, pricing and ad delivery, including disparate impact. Insurance: state regulators police unfair discrimination in underwriting and rating variables. Credit reports: accuracy and adverse-action duties apply under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. A complex model does not excuse specific reasons. Exam tip: for credit A I, look for specific reasons.

2.title: Nondiscrimination Beyond the US, and Managing the Risk
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. E U equality law bans direct and indirect discrimination by race, in employment, by gender, and in access to goods and services. Indirect discrimination is the E U term for a neutral practice with a disparate effect. The G D P R requires fair processing, and the A I Act asks high-risk providers to examine data for bias. A governance routine: define the groups and the metric, test before launch, retest after changes, mitigate, document, and keep human review. Exam tip: indirect discrimination and disparate impact describe the same idea.

2.title: Unfair and Deceptive Practices: Section 5 and State Laws
2.text: Now consumer protection. Section five of the Federal Trade Commission Act makes unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce unlawful, and states have similar laws. Deception is a claim or omission likely to mislead reasonable consumers about something material. Unfairness is a practice that causes or is likely to cause substantial injury that consumers cannot reasonably avoid, and that is not outweighed by benefits. Remedies can include orders, penalties, and deletion of data or models built on improperly obtained data. Exam tip: deception is about what you said. Unfairness is about what you did.

2.title: AI Washing and Claims About AI
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide, tagged verify live. A I washing means claiming a product uses or is powered by A I when it does not, or overstating what it can do. Claims such as accurate, unbiased, human-level or safe need substantiation before they are made. The F T C launched Operation A I Comply in September, twenty twenty-four, and enforces case by case. Fake reviews, undisclosed bots and invented endorsements are deceptive too. At Helios, the claim that the assistant is always accurate cannot be substantiated. Exam tip: an unsupported claim about A I is deception.

2.title: Chatbots, Dark Patterns and Data Practices
2.text: More consumer risks. Presenting a bot as a human, or hiding that a person is talking to A I, can mislead. Dark patterns are interface designs that steer or trap users, such as hidden cancellation, and can be unfair or deceptive. Promising privacy or security and then using data to train models is a broken promise. If a customer relies on a wrong answer, the company's statements and disclaimers matter. Controls: disclose A I use, test claims, keep substantiation records, give human escalation, and review marketing. Exam tip: a disclaimer does not cure a false claim.

2.title: Product Liability Basics: Three Kinds of Defect
2.text: Now product liability. Strict liability for defective products can apply without proof of fault in many jurisdictions. There are three classic defects. A manufacturing defect: the product departs from its intended design. A design defect: the design itself is unreasonably dangerous. A failure to warn: inadequate instructions or warnings about risks. Claims can also rest on negligence and contract warranties. Whether software is a product has been unsettled in U S courts, and the E U has settled it by statute. Exam tip: match the facts to the defect type.

2.title: AI Examples of Each Defect
2.text: Here are A I examples. Manufacturing: a pipeline error ships a corrupted model that behaves differently from the tested one. Design: a triage model is built so that it systematically under-ranks a symptom. Warning: no instructions on the tool's limits, or no warning that outputs may be wrong. The manufacturer or provider answers, and sometimes suppliers and deployers. Updates and learning matter, because a system can become defective after release. Documentation, logs and testing records are the defense. Exam tip: documentation proves due care.

2.title: The New EU Product Liability Directive
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide, tagged dates and verify live. The new Product Liability Directive entered into force on the eighth of December, twenty twenty-four. It applies to products placed on the market from the ninth of December, twenty twenty-six, which is also the transposition deadline. All types of software are covered, including A I systems. Manufacturers can be liable for defects at release and for those that arise through updates, upgrades or machine learning. A product is defective if it lacks the safety a person is entitled to expect. Evidence can be requested. As of the twenty-seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, Member States are still transposing.

2.title: Liability Beyond Defects: The Withdrawn AI Liability Proposal
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide, tagged dates. The Commission proposed an A I Liability Directive on the twenty-eighth of September, twenty twenty-two, to ease claims for harm caused by A I. It withdrew the proposal, announcing it on the eleventh of February, twenty twenty-five, citing no foreseeable agreement. Liability now runs through the Product Liability Directive, national negligence and contract law, and sector rules. Contracts allocate risk: warranties, indemnities, caps and insurance. Exam tip: do not assume a dedicated A I liability law.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. Intellectual property: check the right to use data, through a license, an exception or an opt-out; human authorship for outputs; licenses, trade secrets and confidentiality. Nondiscrimination: disparate treatment and disparate impact; the four-fifths rule of thumb; employment, credit, housing and insurance; the vendor does not carry the employer's duty. Consumer protection: deception and unfairness; substantiate A I claims. Product liability: manufacturing, design and warning defects, and the E U rules that cover software and updates.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A company plans to train a model on text scraped from public websites. Which two steps best manage copyright and data-use risk? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. Rights reservations and site terms can restrict use, and the company needs a documented basis, with records of sources. Public availability is not permission, and reviewing after release is too late.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A screening tool never uses race or sex as an input, yet it rejects a much larger share of one group. Which theory of discrimination most directly applies? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A neutral practice that falls harder on a protected group is disparate impact, and the employer must show the practice is job related and consistent with business necessity.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A screening tool selects forty of one hundred male applicants and thirty-six of one hundred female applicants. What does the four-fifths rule of thumb indicate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Thirty-six percent divided by forty percent is zero point nine, above zero point eight, so the rule does not flag adverse impact. But it is not a safe harbor, and testing continues.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Helios wants to advertise its customer assistant as always accurate, although it has given wrong answers. Which area of law most directly makes the claim a risk? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A capability claim that cannot be backed by evidence is a deceptive practice under consumer protection law. The other areas are not engaged by the advertising claim itself.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. An A I triage tool is built so that it systematically ranks a serious symptom below less serious ones, and patients are harmed. Which kind of product defect does this most closely resemble? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. When the design itself is unreasonably dangerous, the defect is one of design. And the new E U rules expressly cover software, including A I.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all five answers. Question one: A and C. Question two: B. Question three: A. Question four: C. Question five: B. That completes Module five. Next, Module six covers AI-specific laws: the E U A I Act and beyond.
